thread.title: Real estate expert: Regions like Phoenix should stop promoting themselves as low-cost to attract business

author: Mike Sunnucks
title: Real estate expert: Regions like Phoenix should stop promoting themselves as low-cost to attract business
text: – Senior Reporter, Phoenix Business Journal Feb 10, 2018, 5:41pm MST Spencer Levy — head of research for commercial real estate firm CBRE Inc. (NYSE: CBG) — has advice for cities and states trying to recruit jobs and businesses. “Please, please don’t lead with costs,” said Levy, who was in Phoenix last week talking to brokers and clients at CBRE’s modern new offices at the Esplanade development. Low costs have long been a calling card for Phoenix as it competes with the more expensive markets such as California and the Pacific Northwest for jobs and business investment. Levy said regions such as Phoenix and former East Coast and Midwest industrial cities need to ditch that cheap date mentality officials tout as they try to compete with more expensive markets such as New York, Seattle, Los Angeles and San Francisco. “Being less expensive is a long-term loser,” Levy said. The first challenge is there likely is someplace cheaper or offering bigger subsidies. Texas, Florida and Nevada are among the states without income taxes because of their windfalls from energy, tourism and casinos. When it comes to manufacturing, U.S. locations have a hard time competing on cost with Mexico and China. Technology firms can outsource to India or Malaysia and call centers, which are abundant in the Phoenix market, can land in the Philippines or India if they are searching for lower costs. But for the jobs and companies that region want to attract and grow long-term, the keys are talent and innovation. “The big companies don’t look for cost,” Levy said. That’s why Apple Inc . (Nasdaq: AAPL), Facebook (NYSE: FB) and Google parent Alphabet (Nasdaq: GOOGL) are in Silicon Valley. Plenty of technology, creative and financial companies are in expensive real estate markets such as Manhattan, San Francisco and Santa Monica, California. Levy said if Phoenix wants to get in the same economic development class as Dallas, Austin, Atlanta and Boston when it comes to attracting technology and creative companies and corporate headquarters, it needs to focus less on costs. The CBRE research chief, however, is bullish on Arizona State University and Tempe in particular. CBRE ranked Tempe its top submarket in the U.S. for its Tech 30 report late last year. That ranked U.S. real estate markets — suburban and urban — by their technology sector growth. Levy credits ASU with much of Tempe’s appeal and potential. “Arizona State is an enormous driver of this market,” he said. ASU has 100,000 students and has grown its research and development, workforce partnerships and is a real estate engine in Tempe, Phoenix and Scottsdale. ASU President Michael Crow is popular with the private sector, and Levy said that has Tempe poised to be one of the next big college-driven economic and tech hubs in the U.S. He points to how Cambridge, Massachusetts, and Silicon Valley are driven by their links to universities and how Ann Arbor, Michigan (home to the University of Michigan), is an economic engine in the Midwest. “Tempe isn’t Cambridge or San Jose yet, but it’s the next man up,” Levy said. Levy also is optimistic about the Raleigh-Durham area of North Carolina. He sees that as potentially the next ‘it’ region, pointing to its growth potential and universities (University of North Carolina, Duke University and North Carolina State). He also likes Portland with its creative vibe that offers an alternative to Seattle, San Francisco and Silicon Valley. As for Phoenix, Levy groups the region with Denver, San Diego and Nashville. Raleigh is on the 20-city short list for the second headquarters for Amazon.com (Nasdaq: AMZN) along with Denver, Nashville, Austin and Atlanta, as well as more expensive markets such as Boston, New York and Washington. Levy said lower costs also mean lower office rents. That makes lower yields for real estate investors, which doesn’t encourage foreign investment that drive markets such as New York, Miami and San Francisco. – Senior Reporter, Phoenix Business Journal Feb 10, 2018, 5:41pm MST Related Content
